description: Christian teaching on marriage, sexual relationships, family types, and the support of the local parish.
content_html:
Marriage: Purpose and Importance

Christians across denominations regard marriage as the proper context for sexual relationships and family life. The most frequently cited scriptural foundation is Mark 10:6–9, where Jesus quotes Genesis and declares: “Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.” This statement establishes marriage as a divine institution — the bond formed in marriage is not merely a social or legal arrangement but something God himself is involved in creating.

The purposes of marriage in Christian teaching typically include companionship (mutual support between spouses), procreation (having and raising children within a family), and as a framework for sexual relationships that expresses and deepens love. Many Christians also see marriage as a public commitment that reflects the sanctity of marriage — the idea that this bond is holy and carries moral and spiritual significance beyond ordinary human contracts.

Key Fact

Mark 10:6–9: “What God has joined together, let no one separate.” Jesus quotes Genesis and establishes marriage as a divine institution. This verse is the core scriptural anchor for the Christian view of marriage across all denominations — use it in the 5-mark source answer.

Sexual Relationships

1 Corinthians 6:7–20 contains Paul’s teaching that the body belongs to God and is a “temple of the Holy Spirit.” Paul argues that sexual immorality is distinct from other sins because it is a sin against one’s own body, and that Christians should “flee sexual immorality.” This passage is used across denominations to support the view that sexual relationships should be treated with seriousness, though denominations differ significantly on the implications. Traditional Catholics and many evangelical Protestants hold that sexual activity is only appropriate within heterosexual marriage. More liberal Protestant denominations (including parts of the Church of England) have moved to affirm same-sex partnerships and a wider acceptance of sexual relationships between committed couples outside marriage.

On same-sex relationships, Christianity is deeply divided. Conservative traditions cite passages such as 1 Corinthians 6 as prohibitive; liberal traditions argue that the core Christian values of love, commitment and faithfulness apply to same-sex couples as much as opposite-sex ones. The Church of England voted in 2023 to offer blessings of same-sex civil partnerships, a significant development, though it has not yet authorised same-sex marriage in church. Non-religious Humanists and atheists generally argue that consensual committed relationships between adults are morally equal regardless of gender.

Conservative Christians (traditional Catholics, many evangelical Protestants, many Pentecostals) hold that scripture clearly limits sexual activity to heterosexual marriage — 1 Corinthians 6:7–20 and other passages support this. Liberal Christians argue that the biblical context must be read in light of the overriding command to love, and that committed same-sex relationships express love and faithfulness that the Bible endorses broadly. They point to Galatians 3:28 (“there is neither male nor female”) as evidence that equality in Christ transcends biological difference. The honest answer for the exam is that there is no single “Christian view” on same-sex relationships — there are genuinely divergent views within Christianity, and the spec requires students to know both sides and name the sources each uses.

The Purpose and Importance of the Family

Christian teaching holds that the family is fundamental to both the Church and society. Ephesians 6:1–4 instructs children to honour their parents and parents not to “exasperate” their children but to bring them up “in the training and instruction of the Lord.” This establishes the family as the primary place of Christian formation — parents are responsible for the faith development of their children.

Christians in the 21st century recognise that family structures are varied. The nuclear family (two parents and children) is widely held as the ideal in traditional Christian teaching, but the Church also pastorally supports single-parent families, extended families and blended families. Most Christian denominations emphasise grace and pastoral support over condemnation of those whose families do not match a traditional model.

Support from the Local Parish

The local church community supports families through practical and spiritual means. Matthew 19:13–14 records Jesus welcoming children and declaring “the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” — a statement that has shaped Christian ministry to children and families throughout history. Sunday schools provide faith education for children; baptism and confirmation classes prepare families for key rites of passage; marriage preparation courses help couples build strong relationships. Rites of passage (baptism, confirmation, marriage, funerals) also provide the parish community with regular occasions to gather and affirm families at key moments in life.

Key Fact

Ephesians 6:1–4 instructs children to honour parents and parents to bring children up “in the training and instruction of the Lord” — the family is the primary place of Christian formation. Matthew 19:13–14 records Jesus welcoming children and declaring “the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” — the foundation for Sunday schools and children’s ministry.
exam_tip_html: The key sources for this lesson are Mark 10:6–9 (marriage), 1 Corinthians 6:7–20 (sexual relationships), Ephesians 6:1–4 (family duties), and Matthew 19:13–14 (Jesus and children). Use these in the 5-mark question by naming the book, chapter and verse. For the 12-mark Discuss, remember that there are genuinely divergent views on same-sex relationships within Christianity — the exam does not expect you to take a side but to develop both the conservative and liberal Christian positions with named sources and to reach a justified conclusion. A common error is to treat all Christians as holding one view. SPaG marks: sanctity, sacrament, Ephesians, Corinthians.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Mark 10:6–9 establishes marriage as a divine institution: “What God has joined together, let no one separate.” Christians view marriage as a sacred, lifelong bond with purposes of companionship, procreation and sexual fulfilment.
  • 1 Corinthians 6:7–20 teaches that the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit — used by conservative Christians to restrict sexual relationships to heterosexual marriage; liberal Christians take a broader view of committed relationships. Significant divergence exists within Christianity on same-sex relationships.
  • The family is the primary place of Christian formation (Ephesians 6:1–4); the local parish supports families through Sunday schools, rites of passage and pastoral care. Matthew 19:13–14 grounds Christian ministry to children.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Christian beliefs about the purpose of marriage.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete points: companionship — mutual support between spouses (1); procreation — having and raising children in the faith (1); the proper context for sexual relationships (1). Other valid Christian teachings accepted.

practice_questions.text: Describe what Christians believe about the sanctity of marriage.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: marriage is a sacred bond created by God, not merely a human contract (1); Mark 10:6-9 records Jesus declaring 'what God has joined together let no one separate' (1); the sanctity of marriage means the bond carries spiritual significance and should not be broken lightly (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two divergent Christian views about sexual relationships.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per view (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: Conservative Christians (including Catholics and many Protestants) hold that 1 Corinthians 6:7-20 limits sexual activity to heterosexual marriage — the body is a 'temple of the Holy Spirit' and must be treated accordingly (2); more liberal Protestant denominations argue that the core Christian values of love, commitment and faithfulness apply equally to same-sex relationships, and that some Pauline passages reflect cultural norms of their time rather than timeless moral law (2).

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the local church community supports families, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per way; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Sunday schools provide age-appropriate Christian education for children, fulfilling the Ephesians 6:1-4 mandate for parents to bring up children in the training of the Lord (2); rites of passage (baptism, marriage, funerals) are administered by the local parish, bringing families together at key life moments and reinforcing their identity as part of the Church community — Matthew 19:13-14 shows Jesus welcoming children and declaring the kingdom of heaven belongs to them (2); source credit for Mark 10:6-9, Ephesians 6:1-4, or Matthew 19:13-14 named explicitly (1).

practice_questions.text:
'Christians are right to say marriage is the only acceptable context for sexual relationships.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Christian conservative case: 1 Corinthians 6:7-20 teaches the body is God's temple; Mark 10:6-9 establishes marriage as divine; sexual union outside marriage undermines the commitment it symbolises. Counter: liberal Christians argue love and commitment are the core values; non-religious view holds that consensual committed relationships have equal moral value. Evaluate which position is more coherent and why. Secure (7-9): Both sides present, source named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: sanctity, sacrament, Corinthians.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Christian views about same-sex relationships differ, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per view; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Conservative Christians hold that 1 Corinthians 6:7-20 restricts sexual activity to heterosexual marriage — the body belongs to God and same-sex activity does not align with this (2); liberal Christians argue that the command to love is the supreme Christian principle, and committed same-sex relationships can express this love faithfully — they point to the Church of England offering blessings of same-sex civil partnerships in 2023 as evidence the tradition is developing (2); source credit for 1 Corinthians 6:7-20 or Mark 10:6-9 named explicitly (1).

knowledge_checks.q: What does Mark 10:6-9 say that Jesus taught about marriage?
options: Marriage is a social agreement that can be dissolved by mutual consent
What God has joined together, let no one separate
Marriage is only for those who cannot control their desires
Children must be born within two years of marriage

knowledge_checks.q: Which passage does Paul use in 1 Corinthians 6:7-20 to argue for treating sexual relationships seriously?
options: The body is a gift to be shared freely with others
Sexual activity should be reserved for old age
The body is a temple of the Holy Spirit and belongs to God
Marriage is unnecessary for those with strong self-control

knowledge_checks.q: Ephesians 6:1-4 instructs parents to bring up their children 'in the training and instruction of the _____'.
Matthew 19:13-14 records Jesus saying the kingdom of heaven belongs to _____.
Match each scripture to the Christian teaching it supports:
right: Marriage as a divine institution — 'what God has joined together'
The body as a temple of the Holy Spirit — treat sexuality seriously
Parents to bring up children in the training of the Lord

flashcard_questions.q: What does Mark 10:6-9 teach about marriage?
flashcard_questions.a: 'What God has joined together, let no one separate' — marriage is a divine institution, not merely a human contract.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 1 Corinthians 6:7-20 say about the body?
flashcard_questions.a: The body is a temple of the Holy Spirit and belongs to God — sexual immorality is a sin against the body.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Ephesians 6:1-4 say about parents and children?
flashcard_questions.a: Children honour parents; parents bring children up in the training and instruction of the Lord.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Matthew 19:13-14 say about children?
flashcard_questions.a: Jesus welcomed children and said 'the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these'.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the sanctity of marriage?
flashcard_questions.a: The idea that marriage is a sacred, holy bond reflecting God's faithful, unconditional love — not just a legal contract.
Weekly classes during Sunday worship in which children are taught the Christian faith in age-appropriate ways.
A family formed when two adults with children from previous relationships come together.

flashcard_questions.q: What is cohabitation, and how do most conservative Christians view it?
flashcard_questions.a: Living together unmarried — viewed negatively as it lacks the permanent public commitment of marriage.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the liberal Christian view on same-sex relationships?
flashcard_questions.a: Love and commitment are core Christian values that apply to same-sex couples — denomination has been developing.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the conservative Christian view on sexual relationships?
flashcard_questions.a: Sexual activity is only appropriate within heterosexual marriage, based on 1 Corinthians 6 and natural law.

glossary_terms.definition: A lifelong, exclusive union between a man and a woman, considered sacred in Christian teaching and reflecting God's covenant love.
The idea that marriage is a sacred bond that should not be broken — reflecting God's faithful, unconditional love.
Sexual or romantic relationships between two people of the same sex — an area of significant divergence among Christian denominations.
A family consisting of two parents and their children.
A family unit including grandparents, aunts, uncles and other relatives.
A family formed when two adults with children from previous relationships come together.
Weekly classes during Sunday worship in which children are taught the Christian faith in age-appropriate ways.
